sources.note: 'Pistons are made of aluminum alloy having outstanding high-temperature strength.' 'An oil gallery in the form of an aluminum pipe is cast into the upper part of the piston in order to improve the piston's cooling performance.'

sources.title: Toyota Motor Corporation: 1993 Toyota Supra New Car Features (applicable models JZA80 series, U.S.A.; foreword refers to Repair Manual RM343U1/U2), 3. Technical Description, Engine - 2JZ-GTE Engine: Lubrication System, 3. Oil Jets, p. 83 (page scan hosted by mkiv.com)
sources.note: 'there is an oil jet provided for each cylinder. The oil that is sprayed onto the bottom of the piston ... flows into the oil gallery (an aluminum pipe which is cast into the piston) to cool the piston from the inside.'

sources.title: Toyota 2JZ-GTE Engine Specs (engine-specs.net, spec aggregator)
sources.note: 'The pistons are special aluminum casting. Each piston is fitted with two compression rings and a single oil ring.' 'The 2JZ-GTE has an oil spray nozzles to aid in cooling the pistons'.

pistons.note: Toyota does not use the word 'cast' for the piston itself, but it says the cooling-gallery pipe is cast into the piston, which only a cast piston allows; engine-specs.net says 'special aluminum casting'. Oil squirters: Toyota confirms 'oil jets are provided in the cylinder block to cool the pistons' (1993 NCF p. 82), one per cylinder (p. 83). Some tuner pages loosely say 'forged internals'; the piston is a casting. Whether the alloy is hypereutectic is not stated.

sources.note: 'Stock bottom end ceiling: 550–600whp with proper tuning on a healthy engine. Beyond that, you are taking a real risk.' FAQ: 'Sustained high-power use will destroy OEM pistons and rod bolts above 600whp.'

value.note: Lower end of the quoted 550-600 whp range.

reportedLimits.context: Retailer build guide; assumes proper tuning on a healthy engine. Names OEM rod bolts as the first failure point and OEM pistons as limited above about 35 psi.

sources.title: Toyota 2JZ Engine Guide (autopartswd.com)
sources.note: 'With upgraded fueling, a standalone ECU, and a proper tune, many tuners safely push 600–700 horsepower on stock pistons and rods. Some even go higher, though reliability starts to taper off beyond that range.'

value.note: Lower end of the quoted 600-700 hp range; the article does not say crank or wheel horsepower.

reportedLimits.context: Parts-supplier article; needs upgraded fuel system and a standalone ECU; covers stock pistons and rods together. Not corroborated by an independent tuner test.

sources.title: The Legendary Toyota 2JZ-GTE Engine (Tread Magazine)
sources.note: 'Many enthusiasts find that 600–700 hp is the sweet spot for balancing power and durability' and 'Many tuners push 700–1,000 horsepower without opening the block'.

value.note: Upper end of the quoted 600-700 hp 'sweet spot'.

reportedLimits.context: Magazine feature, not a measured test; the 700-1,000 hp 'without opening the block' claim is anecdotal and contradicted by J-Spec Garage's FAQ, which says 1,000 hp claims on stock internals are 'mostly short-duration dyno pulls or unverified numbers'.

Compared with the export engine: ceramic-wheel CT20 turbos, smaller injectors, a milder intake cam and MAP-sensor fuelling (NZ club), which is how Toyota held it to the 280 PS domestic ceiling. The Aristo 3.0V (JZS147) also carried a 2JZ-GTE rated 280 PS / 44.0 kgf·m at 3600 rpm with 8.5:1 compression (goo-net Aristo catalogue), but it is not listed in fittedTo because the NZ club says the Aristo turbos use steel turbine shafts, so it is not verified to be the same hardware.

variants.notes: Same rated power as the 1993-1997 engine, +2.0 kgf·m torque. The NZ club says the VVT-i car also switched from a MAP sensor to a hot-wire air-flow meter. Canada: the 1993 and 1997 NCF tables list Canadian Turbos (Sport Roof only). The 1998 US Turbo was not sold in California-emissions states (Toyota USA).
